claims.text: What the image looks like Eccentric MR jet, dilated LA/LV → mitral regurgitation
claims.quote: Eccentric MR jet, dilated LA/LV Mitral regurgitation

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Valves: morphology, regurgitant jets (color Doppler), gradient/area (CW Doppler)
claims.quote: Valves - morphology, regurg jets (color Doppler), gradient/area (CW Doppler).

claims.text: Chamber sizes: LV (LVEDD, LVESD), RV (> 1:1 with LV = dilated), LA, RA
claims.quote: Chamber sizes - LV (LVEDD, LVESD), RV (>1:1 with LV = dilated), LA, RA.

claims.text: Confirmed by echo: Doppler detects regurgitant flow and pulmonary hypertension; two- or three-dimensional echo shows leaflet morphology and motion, cause and severity, annular calcification, and LV and LA size and function
claims.quote: Diagnosis of mitral regurgitation is suspected clinically and confirmed by echocardiography. Doppler echocardiography is used to detect regurgitant flow and pulmonary hypertension. Two-dimensional or 3-dimensional echocardiography is used to evaluate the leaflet morphology and motion; to determine the cause and severity of MR (see table ), the presence and extent of annular calcification, and the size and function of the LV and LA; and to detect pulmonary hypertension.

claims.text: Acute severe MR may not be apparent on color Doppler; suspect it when acute heart failure comes with hyperdynamic LV systolic function
claims.quote: When it is acute, severe MR may not be apparent on color Doppler echocardiography, but suspicion is raised when acute heart failure is accompanied by hyperdynamic LV systolic function.

claims.text: TEE when endocarditis or valve thrombi are suspected, and to define the mechanism when repair rather than replacement is considered
claims.quote: If endocarditis or valvular thrombi are suspected, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) can provide a more detailed view of the mitral valve and LA. TEE, with 3-dimensional imaging when feasible, is also indicated to evaluate the mechanism of MR in more detail when mitral valve repair instead of replacement is being considered.

claims.text: CXR: acute MR may show pulmonary edema, with no silhouette change unless a chronic disorder is also present; chronic MR may show LA and LV enlargement
claims.quote: Chest radiograph in acute MR may show pulmonary edema; abnormalities in cardiac silhouette are not evident unless an underlying chronic disorder is also present. Chest radiograph in chronic MR may show LA and LV enlargement (see image ).

claims.text: Causes Primary (common causes: mitral valve prolapse, rheumatic fever) or secondary to LV dilation or infarction
claims.quote: MR can be primary (common causes are mitral valve prolapse and rheumatic fever) or secondary to LV dilation or infarction.

claims.text: Acute MR causes: ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture, endocarditis with chordal rupture, acute rheumatic fever, myxomatous chordal rupture, acute LV dilation (myocarditis or ischemia), prosthetic valve failure
claims.quote: Causes of acute mitral regurgitation include the following: Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture Infective endocarditis with rupture of the chordae tendineae Acute rheumatic fever Myxomatous rupture of the chordae tendineae Acute dilation of the left ventricle due to myocarditis or myocardial ischemia Mechanical failure of a prosthetic mitral valve

claims.text: Secondary MR: LV impairment and dilation displace the papillary muscles outward, tethering otherwise normal leaflets so they do not coapt; causes are MI or intrinsic myocardial disease
claims.quote: Secondary (functional) MR occurs when disease of the left ventricle or left atrium (LA) impairs valve function. Ventricular impairment and dilation displace the papillary muscles outward, which tether the otherwise normal leaflets and cause non-coaptation. The causes are myocardial infarction (ischemic chronic secondary MR) or intrinsic myocardial disease (nonischemic chronic secondary MR).

claims.text: Symptoms Acute MR: symptoms of acute heart failure and cardiogenic shock, and specific MR signs may be absent; chronic MR: initially asymptomatic, then dyspnea, fatigue, orthopnea and palpitations (often AF)
claims.quote: Acute mitral regurgitation causes the same symptoms and signs as acute heart failure (dyspnea, fatigue, weakness, edema) and cardiogenic shock (hypotension with resultant multisystem organ damage). Specific signs of mitral regurgitation may be absent. Chronic mitral regurgitation is initially asymptomatic. Symptoms develop insidiously as the LA enlarges, pulmonary artery pressure and venous pressure increase, and LV compensation fails. Symptoms include dyspnea, fatigue (due to heart failure), orthopnea, and palpitations (often due to atrial fibrillation).

claims.text: Cardinal sign: a holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur at the apex, best in the left lateral decubitus position; an S3 at the apex reflects a dilated LV and severe MR
claims.quote: On auscultation, the cardinal sign of mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur, heard best at the apex with the diaphragm of the stethoscope when the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position. In mild MR, the systolic murmur may be abbreviated or occur late in systole. The first heart sound (S1) may be soft (or occasionally loud). A third heart sound (S3 gallop) at the apex reflects a dilated LV and severe MR.

claims.text: The murmur radiates toward the left axilla; it increases with handgrip or squatting and decreases with standing or Valsalva
claims.quote: The murmur radiates toward the left axilla; intensity may remain the same or vary. If intensity varies, the murmur tends to crescendo in volume up to S2. MR murmurs increase in intensity with handgrip or squatting because peripheral vascular resistance to ventricular ejection increases, augmenting regurgitation into the LA; murmurs decrease in intensity with standing or the Valsalva maneuver.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: surgery if symptomatic or EF declining
claims.quote: Surgery if symptomatic or EF declining

claims.text: Chronic severe primary MR: intervention at the onset of symptoms or decompensation (LVEF ≤ 60% or LV end-systolic diameter ≥ 40 mm)
claims.quote: Chronic primary mitral regurgitation that is severe needs intervention at the onset of symptoms or decompensation (left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] ≤ 60% or LV end-systolic diameter ≥ 40 mm).

claims.text: Mitral valve repair is preferred for primary MR; medical therapy or valve replacement for secondary MR; anticoagulants with atrial fibrillation
claims.quote: Mitral valve repair preferred for primary MR Medical therapy or mitral valve replacement for secondary MR Anticoagulants for patients with atrial fibrillation

claims.text: Acute MR: emergency mitral valve repair or replacement, with coronary revascularization as needed; pending surgery, nitroprusside or nitroglycerin and an intra-aortic balloon pump may reduce afterload
claims.quote: Acute mitral regurgitation requires emergency mitral valve repair or replacement with concomitant coronary revascularization as necessary. Pending surgery, nitroprusside or nitroglycerin infusion and an intra-aortic ballon pump may be used to reduce afterload, thus improving forward stroke volume and reducing ventricular and regurgitant volume.

claims.text: Vasodilators have no role in asymptomatic MR with preserved LV function; with LV dilation or dysfunction, an ARB, sacubitril-valsartan, aldosterone antagonist and/or carvedilol is indicated
claims.quote: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and other vasodilators do not delay LV dilation or MR progression and so have no role in asymptomatic MR with preserved LV function. However, if LV dilation or dysfunction is present, therapy using an angiotensin II receptor blocker, neprilysin inhibitor (eg, sacubitril, combined with the angiotensin II blocker valsartan), aldosterone antagonist, and/or vasodilating beta-blocker (eg, carvedilol) is indicated.

claims.text: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) is an option for severe primary MR with NYHA class III or IV symptoms refractory to medical therapy in patients who cannot undergo surgery
claims.quote: Another method of repair is transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) with a device that approximates the mitral leaflets. TEER is an option for patients with severe primary MR and New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III or class IV heart failure symptoms refractory to medical therapy who cannot undergo surgery.
